content_html:
A mutual fund pools money from many investors and charges for running the fund. Some of those costs are obvious, such as a sales charge taken when you buy, but the biggest one is often the yearly expense ratio, which is deducted quietly from the fund's assets. This calculator projects what a mutual fund investment could grow to, shows every fee in dollars and compares the result with the same plan and no fees, so you can see what the costs really add up to.

How to use this calculator

  1. Initial and monthly investment: what you invest today and add at the end of each month.
  2. Annual return before fees: the yearly return you assume the fund's holdings earn. Returns vary, so think of it as a long-run average.
  3. Years held: how long you keep the investment before selling.
  4. Expense ratio: the fund's yearly operating expenses as a percentage of assets, listed in the prospectus fee table.
  5. Front-end sales charge: a percentage taken from each purchase before it is invested. No-load funds charge 0%.
  6. More options: a deferred (back-end) sales charge paid when you sell, and any flat yearly account fee.

How the fees are applied

Every purchase is reduced by the front-end sales charge, so with a 2% load only $98 of each $100 is invested. Each month the balance grows at the monthly equivalent of your annual return, then one-twelfth of the expense ratio is taken from the balance. Any account fee comes out at the end of each year, and a deferred sales charge is applied when you sell, on the smaller of the amount you invested and the ending value.

The total cost of fees is the difference between the no-fee value and your ending value. It is larger than the fees paid because every dollar taken out also stops earning returns for the rest of the holding period. The annual return after fees is the steady yearly rate that would turn your actual deposits into your ending value.

A worked example

Invest $10,000 now and $200 a month for 10 years in a fund earning 6% a year before costs, with a 0.5% expense ratio and a 2% front-end sales charge. You put in $34,000 in total. The calculator shows:

ResultAmount
Sales charges paid$680.00
Operating expenses paid$1,352.15
Ending value after fees$47,687.31
Value with no fees$50,403.17
Total cost of fees$2,715.86
Annual return after fees5.17%

The fees paid come to $2,032.15, but the full cost is about $2,716 once lost growth is included, and the fund's 6% return shrinks to 5.17% for you as an investor.

Ways to keep fund costs down

  • Compare expense ratios between funds that hold similar investments. Over decades a difference of half a percentage point a year adds up to a large sum.
  • Check whether the same fund offers a share class without a sales charge, for example through a retirement plan or a fee-based account.
  • If a fund has a deferred sales charge, find out how it declines each year you hold the shares before deciding when to sell.
  • Look beyond the fees in this calculator: trading costs inside the fund and taxes on distributions also reduce what you keep.

Results are estimates based on a constant return and do not include taxes or inflation.

faq.question: What is a typical mutual fund expense ratio?
faq.answer: Broad index funds often charge well under 0.2% a year, while actively managed stock funds commonly charge somewhere between about 0.5% and 1% or more. The exact figure for any fund is in its prospectus and on its fact sheet.

faq.question: What is the difference between a front-end and a back-end load?
faq.answer: A front-end load is a sales charge taken from your money when you buy, so less is invested. A back-end load, or contingent deferred sales charge, is taken when you sell and usually shrinks the longer you hold the shares.

faq.question: Is the expense ratio billed to me separately?
faq.answer: No. Operating expenses are deducted from the fund's assets, so they are already reflected in the fund's share price and reported returns. That is why they are easy to overlook.

faq.question: Does the calculator include taxes?
faq.answer: No. Mutual funds can pay out taxable dividends and capital gains each year, and selling can trigger tax. Results are before tax, which is closest to how a fund held in an IRA or 401(k) would behave.

faq.question: Why is the total cost of fees higher than the fees I paid?
faq.answer: Money paid out in fees no longer earns a return. The total cost includes both the fees and the growth they would have produced if they had stayed invested until you sold.
